Pure-Play Foundry: A semiconductor manufacturer that only makes chips designed by other companies and never designs or sells chips under its own brand. This avoids competing with its own customers — the business model TSMC pioneered in 1987 and still defines the industry by.
Fabless: A chip company (e.g. Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm) that designs semiconductors but owns no manufacturing capacity of its own, instead outsourcing production entirely to a foundry like TSMC.
Node: Shorthand for a semiconductor manufacturing process generation (e.g. "3nm", "2nm"). Smaller/newer nodes generally pack in more transistors per chip, improving performance and power efficiency — the core axis of competition between foundries.
GAA: Gate-All-Around — a newer transistor architecture (replacing the older FinFET design) that wraps the gate around the channel on all sides for better electrical control at very small scales. TSMC's 2nm node is its first to use GAA.
CoWoS: Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate — TSMC's advanced chip-packaging technology that stacks and connects multiple chips (e.g. a GPU plus its high-bandwidth memory) into one package. It has become a critical, capacity-constrained bottleneck for AI chip production, effectively as important as the leading-edge node itself.
Gross Margin: Revenue minus cost of goods sold, as a % of revenue. For a foundry, this reflects pricing power, capacity utilization, and yield (what % of chips on a wafer actually work).
Operating Margin: Operating income (gross profit minus operating expenses like R&D and SG&A) as a % of revenue — profitability from the core business before interest and taxes.
P/E Ratio: Price-to-Earnings ratio: share price divided by earnings per share. Trailing P/E uses the last 12 months of actual earnings; forward P/E uses analysts' estimated next-12-months earnings. A large gap between the two implies the market expects earnings to grow substantially.
EV/EBITDA: Enterprise Value (market cap plus debt minus cash) divided by EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization). A valuation multiple that, unlike P/E, isn't distorted by capital structure or depreciation policy — useful for comparing capital-intensive businesses like foundries.
ROE: Return on Equity — net income divided by shareholders' equity. Measures how efficiently a company turns shareholder capital into profit.
ADR: American Depositary Receipt — a US-listed security representing shares of a foreign company (here, TSMC's Taiwan-listed shares), letting US investors trade it in USD on the NYSE without directly holding foreign shares.
Capex: Capital expenditure — money spent on physical assets like fabs and equipment. Extremely high for foundries (tens of billions per year) and the main barrier keeping competitors from catching up at the leading edge.
Silicon Shield: The theory that Taiwan's dominance in advanced chip manufacturing is itself a deterrent against Chinese military action — the argument being that a disruption to TSMC would be so damaging to the global economy and technology supply chain that other powers, especially the US, would be compelled to intervene to protect it.
VEU: Validated End-User — a US export-control status that let certain approved foreign chip plants (including TSMC's, Samsung's, and SK Hynix's China-based operations) receive US technology without a separate license for each shipment. This status expired for these companies at the end of 2025.
Section 232: A US trade law provision allowing tariffs to be imposed on imports deemed a threat to national security. Used in January 2026 to place a 25% tariff on certain advanced semiconductor imports, intended to push chip manufacturing onshore.
CHIPS Act: US legislation (signed 2022) providing roughly $52.7 billion in subsidies plus a 25% investment tax credit to incentivize domestic US semiconductor manufacturing — the original policy driver behind TSMC's Arizona expansion.
Beta: A measure of how much a stock moves relative to a benchmark. Beta of 1.0 moves in lockstep with the benchmark; 1.5 means it tends to swing 50% more than the benchmark in either direction; 0.5 means it's less volatile than the benchmark. This report shows beta against both the S&P 500 and the semiconductor sector (SOXX) since the two can tell very different stories.
Volatility: How much a stock's price swings around, measured as the annualized standard deviation of daily returns. Higher volatility means bigger day-to-day price swings, up or down — it's a measure of risk, not direction.
Sharpe Ratio: Return earned per unit of risk taken: (return − risk-free rate) ÷ volatility. Higher is better — it tells you whether a stock's returns are worth the bumpiness required to get them, not just whether it went up.
Max Drawdown: The largest peak-to-trough decline a stock has experienced in the lookback window. If it fell 30% from its high before recovering, that's a 30% max drawdown — a gut-check for how much pain a holder had to sit through, distinct from volatility (which doesn't care about direction).
Short Ratio: Also called "days to cover": total shares sold short divided by average daily trading volume. A rough gauge of how many days it would take short-sellers to unwind their positions at normal volume, and of how bearish (or how heavily hedged) the market is on the name.
